transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thanks. Well, I came in because I just keep losing these huge chunks of time lately. Mostly before I leave the house or right when I'm trying to start my shift. I do IT, so I'm always on the computer, and I'll just sit there re-reading my emails and texts over and over, or I'll keep reopening the same network folders. It’s like I’m trying to prove to myself I didn’t make some serious mistake, you know? 

And I do it with talking, too, mentally replaying conversations. Like the other day, I was replaying this chat I had with a vendor... which reminds me, the vendors we use for our cloud storage are just getting ridiculous with their pricing. I was looking at their invoice and thinking about how much cheaper it was back in 2015. I actually built my own server rack in my garage around then, just with the stuff I learned from my bachelor's degree, just to see if I could. Took me three weekends, but the cooling system was a total nightmare. My neighbor, Dave, kept complaining about the humming noise. Dave complains about everything, though—his lawn is practically a golf course and if one leaf blows over from my yard, he's out there with a rake, glaring at my house. 

But anyway... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, why I'm here. Yeah, I just keep getting stuck doing that, checking my folders and messages so I don't ruin anything.
Do you feel like these thoughts about making mistakes or replaying conversations are intrusive or unwanted?

Yeah, intrusive is exactly the word for it. They just barge right in. Like, even when I'm trying to focus on work—say I'm trying to work through a new system design, or I do some tutoring on the side, so if I'm preparing a lesson—this thought just hits me. It's usually this panic that I sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or that I somehow mishandled these old family photos I digitized, or that I let someone in the community down. 

And speaking of the community, I've been trying to help out at the local rec center, setting up their network, but the router they bought is just ancient. I told the director, "You can't expect gigabit speeds on a piece of hardware from 2008," but he just doesn't get it. He’s a nice guy, though, makes a great chili. They had this chili cook-off last month, and I swear he must put chocolate in it or something, it’s got this really deep flavor. I tried asking him for the recipe, but he just tapped his nose and walked away. 

But, uh, where was I? Oh, the thoughts. Yeah, I just can't seem to let them pass. Even though I know I've already been over it a hundred times, they just won't leave me alone. It's really frustrating.
Do you feel like you have to repeat certain actions or behaviors over and over again in order to feel okay or to prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah, exactly. That's the whole reason I made the appointment, honestly. I have to do it, or I just can't move on with my day. I'll be sitting there before I leave for work, or right before I log on for my shift, and I just start re-reading my emails and texts. Over and over. Or I'll keep opening and closing the same network folders. It's like I have to prove to myself that I didn't mess something up, you know? Like I didn't make some horrible mistake. 

And it's not just the computer stuff, it's the mental replaying, too. Like I mentioned with the conversations. I'll just sit there going over what I said, what they said... which, actually, I was doing that this morning about a conversation I had with the guy at the hardware store. I went in to buy some new weather stripping because the seal around my back door is just completely shot. The wind practically howls through there at night. It's really driving up my heating bill, which is already ridiculous because the gas company raised their rates again in January. They sent out this flyer trying to justify it, talking about infrastructure upgrades, but I haven't seen a single crew working in my neighborhood in five years. 

Anyway... what was the question? Oh, repeating things. Yeah, I have to keep checking the emails and the folders and replaying things in my head, just losing huge chunks of time to it. If I don't do it, I just feel this awful dread that I've ruined something.
Do you feel compelled to perform any specific physical actions over and over, like tapping or counting?

Tapping or counting? No, I don't think so. I mean, I type a lot, obviously, but not like... tapping on the desk or counting to a certain number. Although, I used to have this mechanical keyboard that made the loudest clicking noise every time you tapped a key. Cherry MX Blue switches, if you know anything about hardware. The tactile feedback is amazing, but it was so loud that my ex-wife made me put a towel under it to muffle the sound. 

She had really sensitive hearing, actually. Like, she could hear the refrigerator running all the way from the master bedroom and it would keep her up at night. We ended up having to buy this ultra-quiet German fridge, cost an absolute fortune, and it still didn't even make ice right. The ice maker would just freeze into one giant solid block, and I'd have to get in there with a butter knife every Sunday just to chip away at it so we could have cold drinks. I actually sliced my thumb pretty bad doing that once, bled all over the freezer drawer... 

But, uh... sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the counting things. No, no, I don't do any of that physical stuff. It's really just the checking my screens and the mental replaying I told you about.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge when you're not able to check your emails, texts, or network folders?

I'm not really sure, to be honest. I don't know if I've ever really tested that, because I never let myself get into a situation where I can't check them. I always have my phone on me, or my laptop. 

Actually, I just bought this massive portable power bank to make sure my phone never dies. It's one of those heavy-duty ones, supposed to be 20,000 milliamp hours, but honestly, it takes absolutely forever to charge. I left it plugged in overnight on the kitchen island, right next to the toaster, and it was still only at three bars by morning. 

Which is annoying, but not as annoying as that toaster, let me tell you. It's one of those retro-looking ones, cherry red, really sharp design, but it only toasts one side of the bread. My daughter got it for me for Father's Day a couple of years ago. She lives out in Portland now, works at this artisanal coffee roaster. She sends me these bags of whole bean Ethiopian blends, which are great, but I had to buy a burr grinder just to make a decent cup, and those things are not cheap. Plus they make a huge mess on the counter because of the static electricity... 

Sorry, I completely lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling on edge if I can't check things. Yeah, I don't know what happens if I can't check, because I just always make sure I can. I haven't really noticed what it feels like to be without it since I'm never really away from a screen.
Do you have any recurring, intrusive thoughts that aren't related to making mistakes or replaying conversations?

Yeah, I do. Like, even when I’m trying to focus on my actual job, working through a system design, or preparing a lesson... I do some tutoring on the side for undergrads. Mostly database architecture stuff. Which, honestly, the curriculum they use at that school is a complete joke. I keep telling the department head they need to update it to include more cloud infrastructure, but he's just coasting until retirement. He bought this massive RV, a Winnebago, and all he talks about is driving out to Sedona the second he gets his pension. 

I went to Sedona with my ex-wife years ago. Beautiful place. We took all these physical photos on film... which, actually, I've been trying to digitize our old family photos lately. I bought this flatbed scanner, supposedly high-end, but the driver software is an absolute nightmare on the new operating systems. It keeps crashing every time I try to save a high-res file. I spent three hours on the phone with customer support last week, and the guy didn't even know what a TIFF file was. It's unbelievable what companies pass off as tech support these days... 

Sorry, I'm doing it again. What was the question? Oh, other thoughts. Right. Yeah, so when I'm trying to work on a system design or a lesson, this thought just keeps barging in. I'll get this sudden feeling that I sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or that I completely mishandled those family photos I was talking about, or like I let someone in the community down somehow. And I just can’t seem to let it pass. Even though I know I’ve been over it already and I know it doesn't make sense, the thought just sits there and won't leave me alone.
Do you have any recurring thoughts that aren't about making mistakes, replaying conversations, or work-related tasks?

No, not really. It's pretty much just the stuff I already mentioned. I mean, I guess sometimes I think about what I'm going to make for dinner, but that's normal, right? I've been trying to eat healthier lately, actually. Less red meat, more fish. 

I started buying this wild-caught salmon from a local fish market down by the harbor. It's a bit of a drive, but the quality is night and day compared to the supermarket. The guy who runs it, Sal, he's a real character. Always wears this faded Red Sox cap and tells the worst dad jokes. He was telling me last week about how his son is trying to get a startup off the ground. Something about an app for dog walkers. I tried to give him some advice on their backend architecture, because honestly, most of these startups scale too fast and their databases just collapse under the load. I've seen it a hundred times in my consulting work. They use these cheap NoSQL solutions when they really need a robust relational database...

Wait, sorry. I'm rambling again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, other thoughts. No, no, it's really just the mistakes, the conversations, and the work stuff. Nothing else really comes to mind.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or activities because of these intrusive thoughts or the need to repeat certain actions?

I wouldn't say I avoid things, no. I mean, I still do what I need to do. I go to work, I go to the store... though I have started going to that fish market earlier in the morning to beat the traffic. 

The traffic on Route 9 has gotten completely out of hand since they started that bridge repair project. They said it was going to take six months, but it's been over a year and a half, and they still only have one lane open on the eastbound side. I was talking to one of the construction guys when I was stuck at a standstill last Tuesday. He said they ran into some structural issues with the old concrete pylons. Which, I'm not an engineer, but you'd think they would have assessed that before they started tearing up the asphalt. It's just poor project management. It reminds me of this one software rollout I had to salvage back in 2015. The client had hired this boutique agency that promised the moon but didn't even have a basic staging environment set up. We had to rebuild their entire deployment pipeline from scratch over a holiday weekend...

Oh, I'm sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? Avoiding situations. Right. No, I don't really avoid things. I just deal with the thoughts when they happen, but I don't stop myself from going places or doing things because of them.
Do these intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors cause you a lot of distress or significantly interfere with your daily activities?

Yeah, they do. It's really starting to mess with my schedule. My work has slowed down so much that I've actually missed a few big design milestones lately. And I've had to postpone those mentoring sessions I used to handle without any issues. It's frustrating because I've always prided myself on being reliable. 

Like, back when I was at my first firm, we had this massive server migration. It was a 48-hour marathon over Thanksgiving weekend, and I didn't sleep a wink. I was the only one who knew how to untangle the legacy code they were using. The whole system was written in this archaic version of Perl that nobody touches anymore. I actually have a buddy, Dave, who still swears by Perl. He runs a small web hosting company out of his basement. He’s got these racks of servers just humming away next to his washing machine. His electric bill must be astronomical. He was telling me the other day that he wants to install solar panels to offset the cost, but his HOA is giving him a hard time about the aesthetics. HOAs are just the worst, aren't they? A bunch of busybodies with nothing better to do than measure your grass with a ruler...

Sorry, I lost the thread there. Distress, right. Yeah, it's definitely causing problems. I was actually late and totally unprepared for this youth coding workshop I volunteer for, which really mattered to me. I just felt so embarrassed about the whole thing. It's definitely getting in the way more than I'd like to admit.
Have you noticed any problems in your relationships with family or friends due to these intrusive thoughts or repetitive behaviors?

No, not really. I mean, my wife and I get along fine. She's pretty understanding, mostly. She works a lot too, actually. She's a regional manager for this logistics company, so she's always on the phone dealing with supply chain issues. It's crazy how messed up global shipping still is. She was telling me about this one container ship that got stuck outside of Long Beach for three weeks just waiting for a berth. Three weeks! And it was full of these specialized microchips that go into, like, high-end espresso machines. 

Which is funny, because I actually just bought one of those machines. Not the super expensive one, but a decent burr grinder model. I've been trying to perfect my morning pull. It's all about the tamp pressure, you know? If you don't tamp it evenly, the water just channels right through and you get this sour, under-extracted shot. I watched about ten hours of YouTube tutorials on it last weekend. There's this one guy, an Australian barista, who breaks down the extraction science... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Friends and family? Right. No, no issues there. They haven't really noticed anything, or at least they haven't said anything to me about it. We're all good.
Have you had to take any time off work or significantly reduce your work or social activities because of these intrusive thoughts or repetitive behaviors?

No, I haven't taken any actual time off. I'm still working my regular hours. Actually, I have a ridiculous amount of vacation time banked anyway because our HR department just switched over to one of those "unlimited PTO" policies. Which, if you ask me, is just a clever accounting trick so they don't have to pay out accrued vacation when people leave. It's a total scam. You end up taking way less time off because there's no set number of days you feel entitled to. 

My buddy Greg—he's a senior dev over at a big fintech place—he was telling me their unlimited PTO actually dropped employee vacation days by like twenty percent the first year. He hasn't taken a real vacation since he bought his boat. It's this beautiful pontoon, twenty-four feet, dual outboard motors. We took it out on the lake last summer, and the fish finder he installed on that thing is practically military grade. It uses this incredible sonar mapping software that creates a 3D topographic model of the lake bed in real time, so you can see exactly where the drop-offs are... 

Oh, man. Sorry. I'm drifting again. What was the question? Time off? Right, no. I haven't reduced my hours or taken any time off because of the thoughts. I just keep pushing through.
Have you noticed any difficulties in your relationships or work performance as a result of these intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors?

Well, yeah, like I was saying earlier, work is definitely where I'm feeling it the most. My pace has just crawled. I've missed a couple of big design milestones recently, which is so unlike me. And I've had to push back those mentoring sessions I usually run. I used to handle them no problem, but now I just can't seem to fit them in. 

It reminds me of when I tried to mentor this one kid, Josh, a few years back. Brilliant kid, really, but he refused to use anything but a Dvorak keyboard layout. Have you ever tried typing on one of those? It's completely counterintuitive if you grew up on QWERTY. The vowels are all on the home row, which supposedly reduces finger travel, but it just scrambled my brain every time I tried to help him debug his code. He ended up getting a job at some startup in Austin that makes smart collars for dogs. They track the dog's vitals and GPS, but they also have this feature where it translates the dog's barks into text messages on your phone. Like, "I need to pee" or "Squirrel!" It sounds like a total gimmick, but apparently, they got millions in venture capital. The VC world is just wild right now. People are throwing money at the craziest ideas just hoping one sticks...

Sorry, I'm doing it again. Work performance, right. So, yeah, the milestones and the mentoring. Oh, and I was late and totally unprepared for this youth coding workshop I volunteer for. That really bothered me. I felt so embarrassed because that program means a lot to me. So, yeah, it's definitely causing some friction there.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts are a part of who you are, or do they feel like they're coming from outside of yourself?

I don't know, I've never really thought about it like that. Part of me or outside... it's hard to say. When you say 'outside of myself,' it makes me think of, like, someone beaming signals into my brain. Which, honestly, isn't as sci-fi as it used to sound. 

Have you seen what they're doing with those brain-computer interfaces now? Like Neuralink? They literally had a macaque monkey playing Pong with its mind a while back. It's incredible engineering, but also kind of terrifying. I was reading this piece on Hacker News just the other day about the data privacy implications of neural implants. If a predictive algorithm is anticipating your thoughts to move a cursor, at what point does the thought stop being yours and start being the machine's? My buddy Dave—he works in penetration testing for a cybersecurity firm—he says the encryption on some of those medical Bluetooth devices is an absolute joke. Like, any script kiddie sitting in a Starbucks with a basic packet sniffer could theoretically intercept the data. Imagine getting your brain hacked while you're just trying to order a latte...

Ah, man, I'm sorry. I completely derailed there again. You were asking if the thoughts feel like they're coming from me? I honestly don't know. I guess I'm just not sure how to categorize them.
Do you feel like these thoughts are inconsistent with your own beliefs or values?

Inconsistent with my beliefs? I mean, I guess so? It's not like I actually *want* to be thinking these things. They just sort of pop up and take over. It's like a pop-up ad, you know? You're just trying to read an article and suddenly there's a giant banner for, I don't know, a timeshare in Cabo. 

Which, by the way, my sister actually fell for one of those timeshare pitches a few years ago. She and her husband went down to Mexico for their anniversary, and they got roped into this three-hour presentation because they were promised free jet ski rentals. They ended up signing a contract for a week every February at this resort that looked amazing in the brochures, but when they actually went back the next year, the pool was under construction and the "ocean view" was mostly a view of the parking lot and a dumpster. The maintenance fees alone were costing them more than if they'd just booked a nice hotel. I tried to tell her before she signed, you know, you have to read the fine print on those things. The contracts are designed to lock you in perpetuity. It's almost impossible to sell them on the secondary market because the supply completely dwarfs the demand. There are whole companies now whose entire business model is just helping people legally break timeshare contracts...

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? Uh, beliefs and values. Yeah, no, I don't think these thoughts really reflect who I am or what I believe in. They just... happen.
Have you found yourself avoiding specific places, activities, or social interactions because of these intrusive thoughts?

Avoiding places? Um, no, I haven't really noticed myself doing that. I mean, I still go to the office, still go to the grocery store, still go to the gym... well, I try to go to the gym. 

Actually, my gym just installed these new smart treadmills that have huge touchscreens built into the consoles. You can run virtual routes through, like, the Swiss Alps or the streets of Tokyo while you're jogging. It's supposed to be immersive, but the UI is incredibly clunky. The touch response lags by at least half a second, which is maddening when you're trying to adjust your speed while sprinting. I was looking at the operating system they run on, and it looks like a heavily modified version of Android, but an older build. Probably Marshmallow or Nougat. Which is a huge security risk, honestly, because those older versions aren't getting security patches anymore. If the treadmills are connected to the gym's main Wi-Fi network—which they have to be to stream the video content—someone could easily exploit a vulnerability in the OS to pivot into the gym's main database. They could scrape member data, credit card numbers, all of it. I actually thought about mentioning it to the manager, but he's this guy who wears way too much cologne and always looks like he's trying to sell you a personal training package, so I figured he wouldn't even know what a subnet mask is...

Oh, geez, I'm sorry. I lost the thread again. Avoiding things. No, I don't think I'm avoiding any places or people or anything like that. Just... dealing with the thoughts when they happen.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors are affecting your ability to enjoy time with friends and family or causing problems in your relationships with them?

Well, friends and family... I mean, mostly it's work where I'm really feeling it. My output has just slowed down so much. I've actually missed a couple of major design milestones recently, which is really unlike me. And I've had to postpone these mentoring sessions I do with the junior devs. I used to handle those so reliably. 

Speaking of mentoring, I was supposed to help out at this youth coding workshop last weekend. It's this great program that teaches high school kids Python by having them program these little Raspberry Pi robots to navigate a maze. It's brilliant, really, because Python is such a clean, readable language for beginners, but it still has the power to handle complex logic. But the problem with Raspberry Pis right now is the supply chain. Ever since the chip shortage, trying to get your hands on a Pi 4 is like trying to find gold dust. People are scalping them on eBay for three times the retail price. I was looking into alternative single-board computers, like the Orange Pi or the Banana Pi—which, yes, are real things, they just copied the naming convention—but the community support just isn't there. If a kid gets stuck on a GPIO pin configuration error with a Raspberry Pi, there are ten thousand forum posts explaining how to fix it. If they're using an off-brand board, they're basically on their own trying to decipher a translated datasheet from a manufacturer in Shenzhen...

Oh, right, the workshop. Yeah, I was late to it. And totally unprepared. I felt so embarrassed, because it really mattered to me, you know? But I was just so bogged down in my own head. So yeah, I guess it is causing some problems.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts are something that you would normally think about or are they completely foreign to your own way of thinking?

Foreign to my way of thinking? Oh, absolutely. I mean, I'm a logical guy, you know? I write code for a living. Everything I do is about structure, syntax, cause and effect. If this, then that. These thoughts... they don't follow any logic. They just barge in. 

It's actually a lot like dealing with legacy code. Have you ever tried to untangle a database architecture that was built in, like, 1998? I was consulting for this logistics firm last year, and their entire inventory tracking system was running on this archaic COBOL mainframe. COBOL! In this decade! The original developers were probably all retired in Florida, and the current IT team was just terrified to touch anything because the documentation was practically nonexistent. There were these random subroutines that would execute at 2:00 AM every Tuesday, and nobody knew why, but if you tried to disable them, the whole shipping manifest module would crash. It's what we call "spaghetti code"—everything is so intertwined that pulling one string unravels the whole sweater. We ended up having to build an API wrapper just to get their modern web front-end to talk to this dinosaur of a backend without triggering a cascading failure...

Sorry, I'm doing it again. Tangents. Right. The thoughts. Yeah, they are completely foreign to me. They don't make sense, they don't follow my rules, and they definitely aren't things I would normally sit around thinking about.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts are in line with your own values and beliefs?

Values and beliefs? No, no way. They're the exact opposite of what I believe in. It's actually really disturbing, because I consider myself a pretty ethical, rational person, you know? 

It kind of reminds me of this debate we were having in this online forum I moderate. It's a community for open-source developers, and we were arguing about the ethics of artificial intelligence scraping GitHub repositories for training data. It's a huge issue right now. You have these massive tech conglomerates building these language models—like GitHub Copilot, for instance—and they're training them on millions of lines of code that individual developers wrote and released under specific licenses, like the GPL or MIT license. The argument is whether training an AI on that code constitutes "fair use" or if it's a massive copyright violation. Some guys in the forum were saying, "Hey, it's just learning, like a human would read code to learn," but others were furious, pointing out that these models can sometimes regurgitate exact blocks of copyrighted code without providing any attribution to the original author. We actually had to ban a couple of users because the debate got so heated they started doxxing each other. It's wild how passionate people get about intellectual property when it's their own late-night commits being monetized by a billion-dollar corporation...

Wait, sorry. I'm completely off track again. Values. Right. No, the thoughts don't line up with my values at all. If anything, they go against everything I stand for, which is why they bother me so much.
Are there any intrusive thoughts that are not related to your work, conversations, or daily tasks that you find yourself thinking about repeatedly?

Yeah, there are. Even when I’m trying to focus on something completely unrelated, like... like working through a new system design or preparing a lesson for the junior devs, this thought just keeps barging in. I'll suddenly start obsessing over whether I sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or if I mishandled some old family photos, or maybe let someone in the community down somehow. 

Speaking of photos, it's amazing how much data storage has evolved, right? I was actually trying to digitize a bunch of old physical prints last month. I bought this high-end flatbed scanner—an Epson Perfection, really solid piece of hardware—and I was scanning everything at 1200 DPI because I wanted archival quality. But man, the file sizes! Uncompressed TIFFs at that resolution are massive. I had to set up a dedicated NAS—Network Attached Storage—just to hold them all. I went with a Synology 4-bay enclosure and loaded it with Seagate IronWolf drives, running them in a RAID 5 configuration so I'd have some parity if a drive failed. Because, you know, there are two types of hard drives: those that have failed, and those that are going to fail. The rebuild time on a RAID 5 array can take days if a drive dies, though, and during that time, you're totally vulnerable. Some guys swear by RAID 6 or even ZFS for better data integrity, but ZFS requires so much RAM, and it's really picky about ECC memory...

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. The thoughts about my ex-wife and the photos. Yeah, it just pops into my head, and I can’t seem to let it pass, even though I know I’ve been over it a hundred times already. It just won't go away.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors are significantly interfering with your ability to function in your daily life or causing you a lot of distress?

Yeah, they really are. It's... it's getting bad. My work has slowed down so much that I've actually missed a couple of major design milestones recently. And I've had to postpone these mentoring sessions with the junior devs that I usually handle without any issue. It's just... I can't focus. 

And it's bleeding into my volunteer stuff, too. I help run this youth coding workshop on weekends—teaching middle schoolers the basics of Python and game logic. Python is such a great first language for kids, you know? The syntax is so clean, almost like reading plain English. You don't have to worry about memory management or pointers like you do in C++, which is just a nightmare for beginners. I remember the first time I tried to teach a kid about pointers; their eyes just glazed over. But with Python, you can get a simple text-based game up and running in, like, twenty lines of code. We use Pygame a lot, which is this set of Python modules designed for writing video games. It's a little old-school, but it handles the graphics and sound libraries beautifully. Actually, the biggest challenge with the kids isn't the coding itself, it's getting their development environments set up. We used to spend the entire first day just installing Python and configuring IDEs on these ancient library laptops. Now we just use browser-based environments like Replit, which is a total game-changer. Everything runs in the cloud, so as long as they have an internet connection...

Sorry. Sorry, I'm doing it again. The workshop. Right. I was late to the last one. Late and completely unprepared because I was stuck in my head, doing... whatever it is I do. I was so embarrassed. It's something that really matters to me, and I just couldn't get it together. So, yeah. It's definitely interfering. It's causing a lot of distress.

I'll suddenly start obsessing over whether I sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or if I mishandled some old family photos, or maybe let someone in the community down somehow. 

Speaking of photos, it's amazing how much data storage has evolved, right? I was actually trying to digitize a bunch of old physical prints last month. I bought this high-end flatbed scanner—an Epson Perfection, really solid piece of hardware—and I was scanning everything at 1200 DPI because I wanted archival quality. But man, the file sizes! Uncompressed TIFFs at that resolution are massive. I had to set up a dedicated NAS—Network Attached Storage—just to hold them all. I went with a Synology 4-bay enclosure and loaded it with Seagate IronWolf drives, running them in a RAID 5 configuration so I'd have some parity if a drive failed. Because, you know, there are two types of hard drives: those that have failed, and those that are going to fail. The rebuild time on a RAID 5 array can take days if a drive dies, though, and during that time, you're totally vulnerable. Some guys swear by RAID 6 or even ZFS for better data integrity, but ZFS requires so much RAM, and it's really picky about ECC memory...

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. The thoughts about my ex-wife and the photos. Yeah, it just pops into my head, and I can’t seem to let it pass, even though I know I’ve been over it a hundred times already. It just won't go away.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are causing significant distress or impairment in social or occupational functioning
doctor.question: Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors are significantly interfering with your ability to function in your daily life or causing you a lot of distress?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My work has slowed down enough that I’ve missed design milestones and had to postpone mentoring sessions I used to handle reliably. I also felt embarrassed when I was late and unprepared for a youth coding workshop that mattered to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors are significantly interfering with my ability to function in daily life or causing distress, which directly maps to the Functional Impairment symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, they really are. It's... it's getting bad. My work has slowed down so much that I've actually missed a couple of major design milestones recently. And I've had to postpone these mentoring sessions with the junior devs that I usually handle without any issue. It's just... I can't focus. 

And it's bleeding into my volunteer stuff, too. I help run this youth coding workshop on weekends—teaching middle schoolers the basics of Python and game logic. Python is such a great first language for kids, you know? The syntax is so clean, almost like reading plain English. You don't have to worry about memory management or pointers like you do in C++, which is just a nightmare for beginners. I remember the first time I tried to teach a kid about pointers; their eyes just glazed over. But with Python, you can get a simple text-based game up and running in, like, twenty lines of code. We use Pygame a lot, which is this set of Python modules designed for writing video games. It's a little old-school, but it handles the graphics and sound libraries beautifully. Actually, the biggest challenge with the kids isn't the coding itself, it's getting their development environments set up. We used to spend the entire first day just installing Python and configuring IDEs on these ancient library laptops. Now we just use browser-based environments like Replit, which is a total game-changer. Everything runs in the cloud, so as long as they have an internet connection...

Sorry. Sorry, I'm doing it again. The workshop. Right. I was late to the last one. Late and completely unprepared because I was stuck in my head, doing... whatever it is I do. I was so embarrassed. It's something that really matters to me, and I just couldn't get it together. So, yeah. It's definitely interfering. It's causing a lot of distress.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of intrusive thoughts, repetitive behaviors, and significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning are consistent with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD).
